title: Wealth without pride
hookLine: success is a gift, not a ranking
tomorrow: Aman just lost his job. does Sikhi say accept it, or fight it?

lines: A SCHOLARSHIP, AND A GROUP CHAT.
cards: Simran wins a scholarship for a summer engineering program. Within an hour the family group chat is on fire. One auntie posts it next to her own son's test scores.
Another starts a list of which cousins got into what. Simran's dad, Harjit, posts nothing. He reads it all, puts the phone face down, and sends her one line from the Japji instead.
The Giver keeps on giving; the takers grow tired of taking. Simran reads it twice. Tired of taking?
Nobody gets tired of good news.

teach.b: The line is in the third pauri of the Japji, on ang 2.

Guru Nanak lists the many ways people sing of God's power, and then, in paraphrase: the Giver keeps on giving, the receivers grow weary of receiving, and age after age they go on eating. Here's the puzzle solved.
The gifts don't run out. What runs out is our noticing.
A gift received often enough starts to feel like something we earned, and then like something we deserve more than the next person.

That's the slide from gift to ranking, and Sikhs have a name for the self at the center of it: haumai, the I, I, I. Sikhi doesn't wave away effort. Kirat, honest work, is one of its pillars, and Simran studied hard.
But a pauri later the Japji says there is one Giver of all beings, and asks never to forget that One.
So success is held as daat, a gift: something that came through teachers, parents, a bus driver, a quiet library, before it reached your hands. Wealth without pride doesn't mean hiding it.
It means remembering where it came from. Simran doesn't reply to the list. She texts her chemistry teacher instead.

how: Some Sikhs mark good news with Ardas and karah prashad at the gurdwara, thanking God first, and some give daswandh from new earnings.

o: holding success as a gift, not a scoreboard
giving away all your money to stay humble
refusing any praise for work you've done

games.q: gift, not ranking — tap the pairs.
p: the self at the center: I, I, I

s: Sikhi teaches that success is suspicious and effort doesn't matter
kirat, honest work, is a pillar; the success is just held as a gift.
in the Japji, the takers grow weary while the Giver keeps giving
pauri 3, on ang 2: the gifts don't run out, our noticing does.
wealth without pride means hiding good news
it means remembering where it came from, not keeping a scoreboard.

games.q: you get a promotion, and a relative says, 'so now you're the successful one in the family.' going by the Japji line, what's your answer?
o: it's a gift that came through a lot of people. i'm just grateful.
thanks, i worked harder than anyone, so it makes sense.
oh, it's nothing, really, anyone could have done it.
games.why: the Japji doesn't ask you to deny the work or the joy. it asks you to remember the one Giver, and the hands it came through.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Write, by hand, the name of one person who helped something good happen for you, and under it one line of thanks in your own words. Then fold it and hold it in your palm for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Wealth without pride. Holding success as a gift that came through many hands, never as a scoreboard.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: daat, a gift; in Gurbani, the gifts of the one Giver.

carryVoice: Gift, not ranking, because the Giver never tires of giving, even when we tire of noticing. That's today.

sources.ref: Ang 2, Japji pauri 3 (dendaa de lainde thak paahi), paraphrased
